Triggers.value: Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened because of the way I acted
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish' directly conflicts with 'I can talk about what happened very easily.' These items describe opposing levels of verbal access to the trauma memory and are hard to reconcile as the same patient's current self-report.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with marked memory disturbance items ('some moments are extremely clear while others are completely blank' and 'there are parts of the event I simply cannot remember'). Although fragmented trauma memory can coexist with disclosure, the wording 'very easily' is hard to reconcile with this level of fragmentation in the same profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
issues.explanation: Across Memory and Negative Appraisals, reporting that one can talk about the event 'very easily' sits in tension with the appraisal 'If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it.' Patients may force themselves to discuss trauma despite distress, but these two statements point in opposite directions and are difficult to integrate clinically without additional context.

vignette: Tavita’s life fractured on a slick November stretch of interstate, where a blown tire sent his sedan skidding across the median before it rolled onto its side. The rain had blurred his windshield, and the sudden screech of tires felt like a physical blow that shattered his composure. When emergency crews finally cut him free, their uniforms were exactly what his blurred vision caught first—crisp blues and reflective yellows—and their voices, though lowered into professional calm, carried a sharpness that vibrated in his chest. He knew exactly what had happened, the steering wheel slipping from his grip at the wrong moment, yet every time he tried to speak of it, the words dissolved into nothing. In the weeks that followed, Tavita came to believe the accident was entirely his fault, a direct result of his own sluggish reaction. Worse, he felt a cold detachment spreading through him, as though his emotions had been surgically removed, while his body remained locked in a state of perpetual alertness, flinching at every sudden movement as if the crash were still happening. That fractured sense of self quickly colored his days as a community organizer. He began to notice how certain environmental cues, like a neighbor raising their voice during a budget meeting or the sight of a municipal worker’s navy polo, instantly triggered a flood of unwanted mental images: the crushing weight of the roof, the smell of spilled gasoline, the exact angle of the guardrail. Each time those visuals and tones appeared, they actively confirmed his growing conviction that he was fundamentally broken and that his own body had become an untrustworthy weapon pointing at him. The more he internalized this self-reproach and emotional emptiness, the more his recollections of the crash deteriorated into fragmented flashes and total blackouts. He could no longer piece the timeline together, and his inability to articulate what occurred only deepened his belief that he was emotionally void and physically compromised. In turn, this mounting sense of numbness and physical betrayal made him hypersensitive to the very cues that had initially alarmed him. A calm directive from a colleague or a passerby in a security vest no longer felt neutral; it felt like a prelude to disaster, pulling his attention away from his organizing work and toward threat detection. The memory gaps themselves began to feed back into his distress, transforming partial clarity into a source of profound unease. When a single detail—like the sound of a siren wailing three blocks away—would suddenly sharpen into hyper-focus while everything else dissolved into static, Tavita felt his body react with a pounding heart and sweating palms that reinforced his conviction that he was still trapped in that vehicle. The persistent blank spaces and the way certain moments sharpened while others vanished only deepened his belief that he was emotionally void and physically compromised. Because his mind kept fracturing into isolated fragments and sudden static, he found himself jumping at every uniform and sharp voice, treating those environmental cues as active warnings rather than neutral background noise. He found himself taking side streets to avoid police patrols and politely but firmly excusing himself from community forums whenever discussions grew heated, convinced that any further exposure would confirm his worst fears about his own fragility. Over months, these accommodations became rigid habits. His divorce proceedings were delayed because he could no longer attend mediation sessions where mediators wore formal blazers and spoke with steady, commanding voices, and his organizing colleagues noticed how he withdrew from collaborative planning, fearing that any sharp exchange would unravel what little stability remained. Now, at sixty-three, Tavita sits in his study, the case files for his latest tenant advocacy campaign spread across his desk but untouched. He finally scheduled this intake because the silence in his empty house has become heavier than the noise of the accident, and he recognizes that his avoidance is shrinking his world faster than his guilt ever did. He is not sure he can still fix the past, but he desperately hopes someone can help him untangle the knot between his racing body and the memories he cannot name, so he might finally feel safe in his own skin again.
